comments.author: spillybones
comments.text:
On the other hand, I’m fearful of the damage AI might cause: agent swarms taking over our virtual and physical infrastructure, designing bio weapons. But, back on my first hand, LLMs might also design miracle cures, and come up with clever ways to raise our prosperity.


I really, really object to this framing. Dario Amodei goes particularly hard on the "making bioweapons or curing cancer" framing of AI, and it's complete bullshit. Today's LLMs are good at some tasks and bad at others. They're good at outputting code that looks similar to code in their training data (which can be quite useful), and they're very bad at doing biology work, whether nefarious or benevolent. The argument that LLMs could create a bioweapon or cure any disease depends on so much handwaving and so many assumptions that the "produce outputs similar to its training set" technology will actually be really good at inventing new things if we feed in enough training data and run enough agents. And not only that, but it assumes that the major barrier to curing diseases is that we need a robotic "ideas guy" to output some plausible-sounding ideas. We don't, in fact, have a shortage of ideas to test in medicine. It's actually just extremely expensive, risky, and time-consuming to test ideas.

The fact that so much AI discourse includes bioweapons and medical breakthroughs as talking points is a major feat of propaganda from both the AI salesmen and their close cousins, the Rationalist AI apocalypse cultists. It distracts from productive conversations about the harmful and helpful things that LLMs are actually good at (like finding security vulnerabilities in code).

comments.author: vsvrd
comments.text:
You absolutely need to have a completely accurate mental model of the code.


Developers ought to, yet they don't. I have my own thoughts on whether you need to write the code yourself to build an accurate mental model (writing code is thinking), but even if we accept that we can, my experience shows me that developers do not have the discipline to do so. Charitably, they choose to make the trade-off of maximizing "productivity", which is really delivering work faster that is more or less complete, at the cost of sacrificing correctness, reliability, architecture, and many other characteristics.

One can argue it is an operator issue, or that is it sometimes the right trade-off, but once again, my experience, both my own usage and what I perceive from my colleagues', shows me that the path of least resistance when developing with agents is to accept what they produce regardless of your own understanding or standards, and this is the path the most developers I have worked with appears to follow.

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
Not only in how it works, but also (and even more so!) in what trade-offs there are in different approaches, and what those different approaches even are.


Strong disagree there. Prior to LLMs, the cost of investigating different approaches was so high that the natural instinct was satisficing - explore the problem space until you find something that works well enough, then moving on to something else because you've already spent your allocated time on the problem (and probably more).

LLMs make finding leads on different approaches much easier. Asking an LLM for "options for sandboxing a subprocess on Linux to control filesystem access and memory allocation" is MUCH more likely to give you a good overview of the space than a Google search. More importantly, you can then use coding agents to fire up multiple prototypes of different approaches to help explore the space.

I do this all the time. I don't even need to be sitting at a laptop - I get a lot of my exploratory prototyping done from my phone while I'm walking the dog.

If you're interested in exploring trade-offs and understanding different approaches LLMs are a gift that keeps on giving.

comments.author: gunduzc

I dislike LLMs as much as the next guy, but there exists a small set of errors that are impossible to catch through static analysis (see Rice theorem).

For those, the better solution is having another competent human read your code. Obviously. However, if you don't have access to that, LLMs can sometimes help.

comments.author: threedaymonk
comments.text:
Reading code is static analysis, though, whether it's performed by a human, a static analyser, or an LLM-based tool.

If there are heuristics that an LLM models within that aren't encoded in other static analysis tools, then it might find different bugs, but unless it's actually executing the program, it's subject to the same decidability constraints, and it can't find bugs that can only be found by running the code.

comments.author: kingmob
comments.text:
Yes, though it's not a pure glitch, it has beneficial aspects. Look up Prof. Tomasello's research on the "intentional stance".

Humans evolved to impute intentions to things-not-us, and historically, it worked great to predict fellow humans, prey, and predators. This is despite the occasional false positive (like animism, or "the gods did it").

However, with the advent of the Industrial Revolution, we were able to create machines of sufficient complexity we started anthropomorphizing and ascribing intention to them too. Imagine a railroad engineer fondly saying of a train, "This ol' gal is finicky on the steep grades, ya gotta treat 'er right and not put in too much coal." Or how some people just say "My car/computer/phone/etc hates me" when it regularly doesn't work correctly. AI psychosis is just the latest, most extreme example.

Humans rarely think about how absurd it is to talk about objects like they had personalities. We do it effortlessly.

comments.author: threedaymonk
comments.text:
It seems to be an argument from authority, and when I refer to the article by Jessica Kerr being cited, that starts by assuming the premise. To what degree LLMs are useful is not reported; the author has merely "noticed" it, and why it is "irresponsible not to use them" is not really explained beyond the subjective opinion that they are "more thorough". I'll put "faster" aside, for now: I don't think that it's irresponsible not to use something simply because it's faster. It's not irresponsible to walk when bicycles exist, or to cycle when motorbikes exist.

But this claimed thoroughness is balanced by the problem that the output is no longer understood, and instead of the verum factum of knowing what we have made, it is now generated by a system without its own epistemic model; we have to work to understand the output empirically like the result of some kind of organic process. The proposed solution to this is to write ten times as much testing code, and to instrument everything until methods become twice as long, in the service of these machines.

If we have to produce a lot more code in order to generate code faster, what have we achieved? Is it irresponsible not to want to produce a vast artefact solely for the benefit of a system that can produce large artefacts faster? It's only "irresponsible" if you assume that tests and instrumentation are themselves an inherent good, and having more is ipso facto better.

That is not the case, though: an overlarge test suite that takes too long to run becomes a drag on productivity. There's a resource cost as well, from the LLMs and the CI runners demanding ever more data centres across our dying planet, all so that we can write ever more software that we don't understand, faster than ever before.

I would assert that it is this profligacy that is irresponsible.
